The model response is parsed into two parts: short reflection and an executable action block. The reflection is stored in the trajectory for later analysis but is not executed. The action block is passed to the platform runner, which validates the format and dispatches the corresponding mouse, keyboard, touch, or device-control operation. For desktop platforms, the action block is executed under restricted PyAutoGUI-style sandbox or the corresponding desktop runtime controller. The sandbox permits direct mouse and keyboard control, short waits, and simple control flow, while disallowing hidden automation channels such as shell commands, screenshot APIs, image-location APIs, clipboard-based shortcuts, or application-internal scripting. For mobile platforms, the runner maps the same action intent to ADB-backed Android control or Appium/XCUITest-backed iOS control. For web tasks, browser-facing actions are dispatched through the runtime backend associated with the selected browser and host platform. This keeps the model-facing interaction protocol unified while allowing each environment to use its native execution backend. After each executed action, the environment waits for the interface to settle, captures the next screenshot, and appends the response, action, controller status, and observation artifact to the trajectory. An episode terminates when the agent emits DONE or FAIL, when the task reaches the maximum step budget, or when runtime condition such as step timeout prevents further execution. The evaluator is invoked only after termination and checks the final environment state rather than the intermediate action sequence. D.4 Set-of-Mark Implementation Details Set-of-Mark (SoM) overlays are treated as optional visual grounding aids, not as default benchmark observation. SoM run annotates candidate regions on the screenshot and exposes mark identifiers to the agent. This can help isolate whether model fails because it cannot localize target or because it cannot plan the workflow after localization. Since SoM changes the visual input, SoM results should be reported as an ablation rather than mixed with screenshot-only results. D.5 Result Reporting Protocol Cross-platform result tables are valid only when platform lanes are run under declared task inventory, model registry, observation protocol, action mode, and failure-accounting policy. The report should distinguish task failure from invalid runs caused by runtime setup, model-service errors, or evaluator exceptions. This convention follows the execution-based protocol in the main paper: model succeeds only when the final environment state satisfies the task evaluator, while infrastructure failures are accounted for separately. Recommended reporting ﬁelds. For each model and platform lane, reports include the release version (for example, v1), task count, success rate, invalid-run rate, average steps for successful 46 tasks, timeout rate, observation mode, action mode, and the execution specification used for the run. Aggregate tables separate screenshot-only, accessibility-tree-only, combined-observation, and SoM settings. This prevents visually grounded run from being compared against metadata-assisted run as if the agent received the same information.

sections.title: E Qualitative Analysis
sections.content: Qualitative analysis in OS-OMNI is based on saved trajectories, runtime metadata, and final artifacts rather than isolated screenshots. Each inspected run records the platform lane, task identifier, model, observation mode, action mode, episode status, evaluator result, and the first step at which the trajectory diverges from plausible solution. This makes qualitative inspection useful for separating model errors from benchmark-system failures such as initialization drift, runtime instability, or evaluator mismatch. E.1 Success and Failure Cases Successful episodes typically share three properties. The agent maintains the user goal across application transitions, grounds actions in the current observation, and leaves the target artifact or application record in verifiably saved state. Failed episodes often diverge before the final evaluator is invoked: the agent clicks an adjacent control, overlooks modal dialog, types into the wrong field, loses track of transferred information, or stops after reaching visually plausible but incomplete state. These cases illustrate why OS-OMNI scores final environment state rather than trajectory similarity. E.2 Common Errors by Screenshot-only Agents See Table 8. E.3 Human-Agent Diﬃculty Discrepancies Human difficulty and agent difficulty can diverge sharply in GUI benchmarks. Humans are robust to small UI variations, hidden save states, and modal dialogs, but may be slower on repetitive data-entry tasks. Agents can be efficient when the interface is visually simple and the target state is explicit, but they remain brittle under dense layouts, long-horizon memory requirements, platform-specific shortcuts, and tasks where success depends on confirming saved or exported artifact. For this reason, human studies should use the same initializer and final-state evaluator as model runs, while recording completion time and ambiguity notes. For example, two VLMs may both fail spreadsheet task, but one may misread the screen while the other may identify the correct cell and then fail to persist the edit. Similarly, text-oriented model with accessibility metadata may perform well on labeled forms but fail on canvas-heavy image or diagram tasks. We therefore group inspected trajectories by observation mode, platform lane, task family, and first-failure cause. E.5 Analysis of SoM Eﬀectiveness SoM can improve localization when model can reason over discrete visual marks, but it can also introduce clutter or bias the agent toward marked regions that are not semantically relevant. In OS-OMNI, SoM tests specific hypothesis about visual grounding. It is reported as an ablation rather than replacement for screenshot-only evaluation, because the benchmarks core crossplatform question is whether agents can operate from the same visual signal across desktop, mobile, and web environments.
